Mastering is the last step: the finished stereo mix is made to sound its best **on every system** and
**alongside other records**, and turned into the files that get released. It works on the whole song at
once, with small moves. If something in the mix is wrong (the vocal too quiet, the bass boomy on one
note), go back and fix the mix; mastering can't reach inside.

## Fresh ears

Mastering was traditionally a different engineer in a different room, for a reason: you've heard the
mix a hundred times. Leave it a day. Listen to references. Listen on the speakers you know best.

## Tonal balance

A gentle [EQ](sound-eq.qmd) on the whole mix, compared with a reference:

- Moves of **0.5 to 2 dB**, wide curves. More than 3 dB means the mix needs work.
- Too much low end (muddy, boomy on small speakers), too little (thin), harsh 2–5 kHz, dull top.
- A high-pass below 20–30 Hz removes rumble nobody hears but that eats headroom.

<div class="sk" data-w="eq"></div>

## Glue compression

A slow, gentle [compressor](sound-compressor.qmd) on the whole mix (ratio 1.5:1–2:1, 1–2 dB of gain
reduction, slow attack, release timed to the beat) makes the parts move together. Often done in the mix
already ("mix-bus compression").

<div class="sk" data-w="compressor"></div>

## Loudness and limiting

The **limiter** is the last plug-in: a very fast compressor with an infinite ratio that stops any peak
crossing a ceiling, so the whole song can be turned up.

- Set the **ceiling at −1 dBTP** (*true peak*: the level between the samples, which is what a converter
  or an MP3 encoder actually reaches). This keeps lossy streaming versions from clipping.
- Raise the input until it's loud enough, then **back off**: past a few dB of limiting the drums lose
  their punch and the sound gets flat and tiring.
- Loudness is measured in **LUFS** (loudness units relative to full scale), averaged over the song, which
  follows how loud it *sounds* rather than its peaks.
- Streaming services **turn loud songs down** to a target (Spotify, YouTube, Tidal about −14 LUFS; Apple
  Music −16). A master squashed to −8 LUFS is just turned down to −14, and now sounds smaller than a
  dynamic master at −14. For streaming, around **−14 to −10 LUFS integrated** is plenty; dynamic genres
  (jazz, classical, acoustic) often sit at −16 to −20.

### Hear what over-limiting costs

A looping song through a limiter, measured the way streaming services measure it (LUFS, with a true-peak
reading). Play it, then compare **Dynamic** with **Crushed**: the crushed one is louder, and has lost its
punch. Now switch **streaming normalisation** on: both are turned to the same level, and the crushed one
is simply smaller. Watch the *peak-to-loudness* figure shrink as the drive goes up.

<div class="rk" data-w="loudness"></div>

## Stereo and mono

Check in **mono** ([Sound 23: Stereo](sound-stereo.qmd)): the vocal and bass must stay solid. Keep the
bass (below ~120 Hz) in the centre; wide bass cancels on mono systems and cuts badly on vinyl. More on mono playback, one earbud, live sound and subwoofers in
[Recording 7: Mono and Stereo](rec-stereo.qmd).

## Finishing

- **Sequence** an album: the order, the gaps, matching levels so no song jumps out.
- **Fades** at the start and end; trim silence.
- **Dither** when reducing to 16-bit (CD, some distributors): a tiny noise that replaces the
  distortion of rounding. Only once, at the very end.
- **Files**: a 24-bit WAV at the mix's sample rate for streaming distributors, a 16-bit/44.1 kHz WAV
  for CD, and an MP3 for the band's phones.
- **Metadata**: title, artist, ISRC codes if you have them.
